checks.result: Scale check. On the plain ratio, sampled random valid answers average above 0.5 on 6 instances (myciel3, games120, miles500, miles750, miles1000, miles1500), and every valid answer is above 0.5 on 4, so the ratio is not used. On the scale used they average 0.119 over all instances, at most 0.376 on one, and none is above 0.5.

open_issues: The zero of the score is the worst valid value (largest degree + 1 colours), not the expected value of a uniformly random valid answer that R2 asks for. That expectation needs the chromatic polynomial and cannot be computed exactly. The scale is therefore more lenient than R2's: sampled random valid answers average 0.12 on it (group means: REG 0.27, book 0.26, miles 0.14, MYC 0.08, queen 0.06, LEI 0.01, game 0.00), at most 0.38 on one instance.

An exact alternative zero exists and was not chosen: the expected colour count of a uniformly random answer that need not be valid, K(1-(1-1/K)^n). It lies below what random valid answers reach (miles1500: 74.8 against about 94 sampled, reference 73) and would make that instance nearly all-or-nothing. An auditor may prefer it.

The answer form offers largest degree + 1 colours. A proper colouring that uses more cannot be written in the form. score() accepts any non-negative colour labels and gives such a colouring 0, the same as any answer using largest degree + 1 colours, so nothing that could score is excluded. Strictly, though, not every valid published answer is expressible.

Group [0], colours in use, is a function of the partial assignment (it rises by 1 when a vertex takes a colour no assigned vertex has). It is not literally a sum of fixed terms each reading a fixed set of variables. It follows the existing bin packing adapter, which counts bins in use the same way, and it is exact for complete answers.

The size limit MAX_CELLS = 100,000 on vertices*(largest degree + 1) is about three times the preferred 30,000. I first wrote 64,000, saw that the kernel's split then had 15 training instances, and raised it to the round limit at which it has 16. That was after looking at sizes and the split and before any answer was scored. Ten used instances exceed 30,000 (largest: le450_25c at 81,000). Under a strict 30,000 only 33 instances remain.

Attainability of the reference is not verified by me for le450_15c, le450_15d, le450_25c and le450_25d; three of them (15c, 15d, 25d) are among the 16 training instances. There the reference rests on the page alone ('Leighton graphs with guaranteed coloring size'). All 24 fresh instances have a verified attaining colouring.

The split is lopsided in kind and size. Training is 11 Leighton graphs of 450 vertices plus 5 miles graphs; fresh is Mycielski, register allocation, book, game and queen graphs of 11 to 211 vertices. SGB-game is a group of one instance.
The score is coarse on small instances: myciel3 has 6 colours on offer and reference 4, so its only scores are 0, 0.5 and 1; games120 has 14 on offer and reference 9.

With only 6 made-up graphs, design a reported 'the budget did not allow one round of learning' at the registered budget; with 16, as the kernel uses, it learns. This is the learner's planning, seen as a black box, not an interface fault.
The page's HTML is malformed around latin_square_10 and le450_15a (a broken link). The adapter reads names from the visible text, and the file URL follows the documented pattern instances/<name>.col.
The threshold 0.90 is an operating point with no external anchor. I did not compute how any heuristic or the learner scores on the benchmark to set it.

answer_form: AssignProblem. One variable per vertex and one option per colour. The number of options is instance data: largest degree + 1. It is unordered, has no capacity (a colour may be taken by any number of vertices), no domain and no start answer. The only exposed array is one var_var relation, the 0/1 adjacency matrix built from the 'e' lines. There are no attribute columns. Vertices and colours are both relabelled by the seed, and decode maps an answer back to the file's vertex order.
groups: Term groups: [0] the number of colours in use by the assigned vertices (soft; for a complete answer it is the published value); [1] the number of edges whose two assigned ends share a colour (hard). Instance groups are the page's source codes, with SGB divided as the page itself divides it: LEI 12, REG 8, SGB-queen 8, MYC 5, SGB-miles 5, SGB-book 4, SGB-game 1.
instances_left_out: 36 of the page's 79 instances, by four rules stated in the module text. (1) Only in the binary .col.b format, 21: the 12 DSJC, 3 DSJR and 6 flat graphs. (2) The page prints '?' instead of a number, so there is no reference, 8: latin_square_10, school1, school1_nsh, queen10_10, queen12_12, queen14_14, queen15_15, queen16_16. (3) More than 500 vertices, 4: inithx.i.1, inithx.i.2, inithx.i.3, homer. (4) vertices*(largest degree + 1) above 100,000, 3: fpsol2.i.1 (125,488), fpsol2.i.2 (156,497), fpsol2.i.3 (147,475).
reference: The number printed beside each instance under 'optimal coloring' on the pinned page instances.html, which is the chromatic number. It is attainable by definition and never exceeds largest degree + 1. It is read only by score() and reference(). My own search found a colouring with exactly that number for 39 of the 43 instances; for le450_15c, le450_15d, le450_25c and le450_25d it rests on the page alone.
score_scale: Not the plain ratio. The score is the share of the way from the worst valid value of the form (largest degree + 1 colours, which a valid answer does attain) to the page's number: (worst - used)/(worst - number), cut to [0, 1]. It is 1 when the number is reached or beaten and 0 for a conflict or a malformed answer. The ratio was rejected because it cannot fall below number/(largest degree + 1), which is above 0.5 on four instances (0.68 on miles1500), and sampled random valid answers average above 0.5 on six. The zero R2 asks for, the expected value of a uniformly random valid answer, is not exactly computable here, so the exact worst valid value is used instead; this is more lenient (see open issues).
source: Graph Coloring Instances page of M.
